content.value_statement: Vague commit messages make reviews and project history difficult to understand. This skill examines staged changes and guides you to concise Conventional Commit messages with clear context.
actual_capabilities: Reviews staged Git diffs to identify the main change.
Suggests Conventional Commit types such as feat, fix, docs, and refactor.
Helps define a focused scope and imperative summary.
Provides examples for feature, fix, refactor, and infrastructure commits.
Explains how to document breaking changes in commit messages.
Guides selective staging and commit amendment workflows.
limitations: It does not run tests or verify that the staged code is correct.
It cannot determine project-specific commit rules unless you provide them.
It suggests messages but does not guarantee repository policy compliance.
It does not replace review of sensitive changes before committing.

use_cases.title: Prepare a first commit
use_cases.description: Turn a small staged change into a concise Conventional Commit message.

use_cases.title: Improve team history
use_cases.description: Create consistent messages that make release notes and code history easier to review.

use_cases.title: Describe a broad refactor
use_cases.description: Summarize related multi-file changes and identify any breaking impact.

prompt_templates.title: Create a basic message
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my staged changes and suggest one Conventional Commit message.

prompt_templates.title: Explain the recommendation
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze my staged diff. Suggest a commit type, scope, and summary, then explain each choice.

prompt_templates.title: Document a feature
prompt_templates.prompt: Review the staged changes for this feature. Write a Conventional Commit subject and body that explain the user impact.

prompt_templates.title: Review a breaking refactor
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze my staged refactor. Propose a complete Conventional Commit message, identify breaking changes, and list assumptions that need confirmation.

output_examples.input: Staged changes add email validation to the account form.
output: Suggested message: fix(form): validate account email
Reason: The change corrects form validation behavior in a focused area.

output_examples.input: Staged changes add rate limiting to API endpoints.
output: Suggested message: feat(api): add rate limiting
Optional body: Protect API endpoints from excessive requests and provide predictable client behavior.

output_examples.input: Staged changes change an API response structure.
output: Suggested message: feat(api)!: restructure response format
Footer: BREAKING CHANGE: Clients must read the new response fields.

best_practices: Review the staged diff before accepting a suggested message.
Keep each commit limited to one logical change.
Use the body to explain why a non-obvious change is needed.
anti_patterns: Do not commit unrelated changes under one broad message.
Do not use vague subjects such as update or fix stuff.
Do not mark a breaking change as compatible.

faq.question: Does this skill create commits?
faq.answer: It guides message creation and documents Git commands. Review the command before running it.

faq.question: What format does it use?
faq.answer: It follows the Conventional Commits format with type, optional scope, summary, body, and footer.

faq.question: Can it review unstaged files?
faq.answer: The primary workflow focuses on staged changes. Stage the intended files before requesting a message.

faq.question: Can I use custom commit types?
faq.answer: Yes. Provide your repository convention, and use it to guide the suggested message.

faq.question: How are breaking changes shown?
faq.answer: Use an exclamation mark after the type or scope and add a BREAKING CHANGE footer when appropriate.

faq.question: Should I accept every suggestion?
faq.answer: No. Confirm that the message accurately reflects the change and your team requirements.
